advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Clamp/validate free_watermark_pct to a sane 0..100 domain (and warn on out-of-range) so a large value cannot make the trigger exceed the volume and cause unconditional eviction.
evidence: No clamping/validation of free_watermark_pct exists in _space_thresholds, JanitorConfig, or _snapshot_int (which only int-coerces).
JanitorConfig docstring only says values are integers/whole points; no stated 0..100 domain enforcement.
advisory.finding: free_watermark_pct has no upper-bound validation; a value >=100 (or pct+RECLAIM_TARGET_MARGIN_PCT>=100) makes total*pct//100 >= total, so trigger >= total volume size and `free < trigger` is always true — the janitor would evict aggressively on every pass regardless of real disk pressure, and the target may be unreachable, causing it to reclaim down to nearly empty.
scenarios: Operator misconfigures REBAR_GATE_FREE_WATERMARK_PCT to 100 (or a typo like 200 meaning 20)
free_watermark_pct set to 96+ so pct+margin exceeds 100 and target becomes unreachable

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Consider defaults.get(key) with an explicit error or documented contract that the defaults mapping MUST contain the key, so a missing key fails loudly by design rather than incidentally.
evidence: Old signature: `def _snapshot_int(raw: str | None, table: dict, file_key: str, default: int) -> int:` returned scalar `default`.
All in-tree callers route through _default_tunables() which includes every key, so no live break; risk is for future/other callers.
advisory.finding: _snapshot_int now returns defaults[key] and will raise KeyError if the passed defaults mapping lacks the resolved key, whereas the previous signature always received an explicit scalar default and could never KeyError. Any caller passing a defaults dict missing a key now fails hard instead of falling back.
scenarios: A future caller (or refactor) passes a partial defaults mapping expecting per-knob fallback

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a _space_thresholds/run_gc case where the absolute floor exceeds the volume-relative term (e.g. small free_watermark_pct or large free_watermark_bytes) and assert the trigger equals the absolute floor.
evidence: janitor.py:339-341 docstring: 'Each is the larger of the absolute floor and the volume-relative term, so raising one term can never weaken the other.'
All new pct tests use `free_watermark_pct=20` on `_ROOT_TOTAL = 30 * _GIB` -> volume term 6 GiB > 2 GiB absolute floor, so max() never selects the absolute floor.
ABSENCE: no test sets free_watermark_bytes high or free_watermark_pct low such that the absolute floor > volume-relative term, so the absolute-floor-as-hard-minimum branch of max() is unverified.
advisory.finding: The core documented contract of _space_thresholds — the trigger/target is the LARGER of the absolute floor and the volume-relative term, so 'raising one term can never weaken the other' — is only tested in the direction where the volume-relative term dominates. Every pct-enabled test uses free_watermark_pct=20 on a 30-GiB volume (30*20//100 = 6 GiB), which always exceeds the 2-GiB absolute floor, so the max() always resolves to the percentage term. No test exercises the case where the absolute floor is the larger term (e.g. a small percentage or a large free_watermark_bytes), so a regression replacing max(...) with the volume-relative term alone (dropping the absolute-floor guarantee) would pass all tests.
scenarios: A refactor that computes trigger = total * pct // 100 without the max() would leave the absolute floor unguaranteed and still pass CI.
advisory.suggested_fix: Add a test with free_watermark_pct=1 (or a large free_watermark_bytes) on the 30-GiB volume asserting eviction still triggers at the absolute-floor free level and that target/trigger collapse to free_watermark_bytes when the percentage term is smaller.
